en: Thus have I heard: The Middle Discourses 47: The Discourse on the Investigator (Vīmaṁsakasutta) Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is an investigator, not knowing the way of another’s mind, should examine a Tathāgata for the sake of discerning whether he is a Perfectly Enlightened One or not.”
“Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, and have the Blessed One as their refuge.
It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One himself would explain the meaning of this statement; having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.
“In that case, bhikkhus, listen and attend closely; I shall speak.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:

“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu who is an investigator does not know another’s mind, he should examine the Tathāgata with respect to two kinds of phenomena—phenomena cognizable by the eye and the ear: [namely,] whether he is one who speaks at the right time, speaks what is true, speaks what is beneficial, and speaks with a mind of loving-kindness.”
‘Are those phenomena cognizable by the eye and ear that are defiled present in the Tathāgata or not?
Examining him, he knows thus:
‘Those phenomena cognizable by the eye and ear that are defiled are not present in the Tathāgata.’
When, upon investigating him, he knows thus:
"Those defiled states cognizable by the eye and the ear do not exist in the Tathāgata," he then investigates further:
"Do those mixed states cognizable by the eye and the ear exist in the Tathāgata or not?"
Investigating him, he knows thus:
‘Those phenomena cognizable by the eye and ear that are mixed [with the unwholesome] do not exist in the Tathāgata.
When, investigating him, he knows thus:
‘Those phenomena cognizable by the eye and ear that are mixed, those do not exist in the Tathāgata,’ he then investigates further:
‘Do those phenomena cognizable by the eye and ear that are pure exist in the Tathāgata, or do they not?
As he investigates him, he knows thus:
‘Those pure phenomena cognizable by the eye and the ear exist in the Tathāgata.
When, upon investigation, he knows thus:
‘Those pure phenomena cognizable by the eye and the ear exist in the Tathāgata,’ he investigates him further beyond that:
‘Has this venerable one attained this wholesome state for a long time, or has he attained it only recently?
Examining him, he comes to know:
‘This venerable one has attained this wholesome state for a long time; this venerable one has not attained it only recently.’
When, upon investigating him, he knows thus:
"This venerable one has long been established in this wholesome state; this venerable one is not one who has attained it only for a short time," he then investigates him further:
"Has this venerable bhikkhu reached renown and attained fame, and are there certain dangers present here for one who possesses such status?"
“Monks, as long as a monk has not attained renown and achieved fame, certain dangers do not yet manifest for him here.
But when, monks, a monk has attained renown and achieved fame, then certain dangers do manifest for him here.
Examining him, one knows this:”
‘This venerable bhikkhu has been approved by the formal motion and has attained fame; no faults whatsoever are found in him here.
When, while investigating him, he knows thus:
‘This venerable bhikkhu has been approved by the formal motion and has attained fame; no faults whatsoever are found in him here,’ then he investigates him further:
‘This venerable one has abstained out of fearlessness; this venerable one has not abstained out of fear.
Because he is free from lust, he does not indulge in sensual pleasures, owing to the destruction of lust.
Examining him, he knows thus:
‘This venerable one has abstained out of fearlessness; this venerable one has not abstained out of fear.
Because he is free from lust, he does not indulge in sensual pleasures, for lust has been destroyed.
If, monks, others were to ask that bhikkhu thus:
“What are the venerable one’s reasons, what are his grounds, by which he says this:
‘This venerable one has desisted out of fearlessness; this venerable one has not desisted out of fear;
because he is free from lust, he does not pursue sensual pleasures, owing to the destruction of lust’?”
Answering rightly, monks, a monk should answer thus: ‘For this venerable one,
whether living in the Saṅgha or living alone, [regards] those there who are well-gone and those there who are ill-gone,
those there who instruct a group, and those here who are seen to be intent on material things.’
And as for those here who are unstained by worldly gain, this venerable one does not despise them on that account.
Furthermore, I have heard and received this directly from the Blessed One:
"I am abstinent through fearlessness; I am not abstinent out of fear. Because I am free from lust, I do not pursue sensual pleasures, for lust has been destroyed."
In this matter, monks, the Tathāgata alone should be questioned further:
“Do those phenomena cognizable by the eye and the ear that are defiled exist for the Tathāgata, or do they not?
Being asked, monks, the Tathāgata would answer thus:
‘Those phenomena cognizable by the eye and ear that are defiled do not exist in the Tathāgata.
‘As for those phenomena cognizable by the eye and ear that are mixed, do they exist in the Tathāgata or not?
In answering, monks, the Tathāgata would answer thus:
‘Those phenomena cognizable by the eye and ear that are mixed, those do not exist in the Tathāgata.
‘Do those phenomena cognizable by the eye and ear that are pure exist in the Tathāgata or not?
In answering, monks, the Tathāgata would answer thus:
‘Those pure phenomena cognizable by the eye and the ear exist in the Tathāgata;
this is my path, this is my domain, yet I am not made of that.
A disciple, monks, ought to approach such a teacher to hear the Dhamma.
The Teacher teaches him the Dhamma in a way that is progressively higher and more sublime, contrasting the dark with the bright. Monks,
as the Teacher teaches the Dhamma to a monk in a way that is progressively higher and more sublime,
contrasting the dark with the bright, so too does he, through direct knowledge of that Dhamma, here [realize] a certain state.
He reaches a conclusion regarding phenomena and gains confidence in the Teacher, thinking:
“The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened; the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One;
the Saṅgha has practiced the good way. Monks, if others should ask that monk:
“By what characteristics, by what reasons does the venerable one say:
‘The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened; the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One; the Saṅgha has practiced the good way’?
Monks, answering correctly, a monk should answer thus:
“Here, friends, I approached the Blessed One to hear the Dhamma.
The Blessed One taught me the Dhamma—progressively higher and more sublime, dealing with the contrast between the dark and the light.
Just as the Blessed One taught me the Dhamma, progressively higher and more sublime, dealing with the contrast between the dark and the light...”
"In such and such a way, having directly known that Dhamma, I reached a conclusion regarding certain phenomena among all phenomena, and I gained confidence in the Teacher:
‘The Blessed One is a perfectly awakened Buddha; the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One; the Saṅgha has practiced the good path.
Monks, whoever has faith in the Tathāgata through these aspects, these phrases, and these syllables...

It is settled, rooted, and established; this, monks, is called faith that is well-founded, rooted in vision, firm, and unshakable by any ascetic or brahmin, by any deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world.
In this way, monks, there is an investigation of the Dharma regarding the Tathāgata.
"And thus the Tathāgata is well-established in the nature of things (dhammatā).
This is what the Blessed One said.
Elated, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Vīmaṁsaka Sutta, the seventh, is finished.
